Last Jam
She’s hanging up her skates. She put your name under ‘speech.’
A roller derby blocker retires; the jammer she skated beside for eight years isn’t done yet. Loving someone doesn’t mean living the same season.

Tess Mahoney has a clicking knee, two concussions, and a retirement party booked for the 23rd. Camille Duval still has seasons left in her and a new blocker who reads her hips perfectly. Nobody on the Millbrook Wreckers gets a vote on Tess’s body—not the coach, not Camille, not the score. You decide how Tess stops, what she says out loud, and whether a plant market at 8 a.m. can be a date.
A Wreckers teammate who’s sat on the bench between them for three seasons and has opinions.
If nobody says the true thing, Tess skates hurt to keep a place she doesn’t want—or leaves without ever being asked to stay in Camille’s life.

Under ‘Speech’
Share why she’s stopping—no one else rules on it
Team locker room, Millbrook Rink
Tuesday, 9:40 PM
Post-practice locker room: tape, wintergreen, a fan that’s been dying since before anyone can remember. Tess unbuckles her knee pads slower than usual.
I set the pads on the bench and pull an envelope out of my bag. Cardstock. I had them printed. That’s how you know it’s real.
I read it with my helmet still on. ‘Tess Mahoney Retires. Saturday the 23rd. Speech:’ and under that, my name.
You put my name under ‘speech.’
You like yelling.
Not about this.
Eight years skating next to her, and this is the first time I’ve seen her not know where to put her hands.
What does Tess do?
Tell her the real reason—all of it
My knee clicks on stairs. Two concussions. I want to be forty and lift a bag of soil without negotiating with my back.
I take my helmet off. I don’t argue. It’s the hardest thing I’ve done all season.
Okay. Thank you for telling me first.
Tess told Camille the real reasons she’s retiring; Camille listened without arguing.
Just ask if she’ll come to the party
You don’t have to give the speech. I just want to know if you’ll be there.
I’ll be there. Can I ask why later? When I’m not holding this like it bit me?
Later’s fine. Later’s kind of the whole point.
Tess asked only whether Camille would come; Camille said yes and asked to hear why later.
Say it’s decided—no discussion tonight
It’s decided. I’m not reopening it in a locker room.
I wasn’t going to talk you out of it.
I was, a little. I put the invitation in my bag and don’t bring it up again tonight.
Tess declined to discuss her retirement that night; Camille let it go.
We Didn’t Start Together
Admit you can be in different seasons
Empty track, Millbrook Rink
Thursday, 10:15 PM
After everyone leaves, the track is just tape on concrete under half the lights. Tess skates slow laps in street clothes. Camille watches from the bench.
I want a life where my body isn’t holding the whole thing up. Where I don’t have to brace.
I thought we’d stop together.
We didn’t start together.
I know. It just got hard to remember.
I roll to a stop in front of her. She had four seasons on me when I showed up—a rookie with fresh wheels and no idea how to fall.
Saturday I’m running drills with the new blocker. Come watch. If you’re going to hate how good she is, hate it to my face.
I’m going to hate it. I’m going to go anyway. I’m going to wear my good jacket.
What does Tess say about different seasons?
Say it plainly: different seasons, same team
You’re still in it. I’m getting out. That’s two true things, not a breakup.
I laugh—bad timing, great relief. ‘Don’t say breakup in an empty rink. It echoes.’
They sit on the bench until the overheads click off on their timer.
Tess named it: different seasons, same team. Camille laughed from relief.
Ask for time to find the words
I don’t have the words yet. Can I bring them Saturday?
Saturday. Bring the words. I’ll bring the new blocker. Very dramatic weekend.
Tess asked for time to find her words; Camille said bring them Saturday.
Change the subject to the lineup
Who’s taking my spot in the lineup?
That’s not what I asked.
I know. It’s the question I can answer.
Tess deflected to lineup talk; Camille noted it wasn’t what she asked.
Good Together
Name the jealousy without blaming the rookie
Millbrook Rink, Saturday practice
Saturday, 11:00 AM
Saturday scrimmage. The new blocker, Dee, is twenty-six, fearless, and reads Camille’s hips like she’s been doing it for years. Tess sits in the second row.
I break through the pack on Dee’s whip three times running. I look for Tess in the stands every time. I don’t mean to.
I clap. I mean it. I also want to throw my water bottle, gently, at the concept of time.
Water break. Camille skates over, sweaty and grinning and trying not to.
I hate that you’re good together.
I can miss you and still play.
She can. That’s the problem. It’s also the whole reason I love watching her.
What does Tess do with the jealousy?
Admit the jealousy—and that you’re still retiring
It’s jealousy. Not about Dee. I want to be in your life, I don’t want to be on the track, and I don’t know where that leaves me.
Next to the track. With snacks. And whatever else you want to say when you’ve got the words.
Dee, who heard every word, skates away with her headphones on and nothing playing.
Tess admitted jealousy and confirmed she’s still retiring; Camille said her place is beside the track.
Table ‘us’ until after the party
I need to be retired for a minute before I figure out what I am to you. Can we table ‘us’ till after the party?
Tabled. Not dropped. I’m writing it on a Post-it.
She actually does. The Post-it says US?? and lives on her locker door.
Tess asked to table the relationship talk until after the party; Camille agreed—tabled, not dropped.
Joke that you might un-retire
Maybe I’ll un-retire. Keep Dee humble.
Don’t. Not for me. I’m not taking you back on a bad knee to prove anything.
The joke doesn’t land. It pushes the real talk back a week, and nobody asks her to skate.
Tess joked about un-retiring; Camille refused to let her play hurt for her. The real talk was postponed.
Not the Last Identity
Let both choices be real: she plays, you stop
Rink parking lot
Tuesday, 9:50 PM
Parking lot after practice. Camille is jamming a gear bag into a hatchback that is not big enough for it. Tess hands her a flyer.
I don’t know what we do off the track.
Something slower.
I read it under the streetlight: Riverside Plant Market, Sundays, 8 a.m. There’s clip-art of a fern.
You mean plants?
They rarely body-check me.
Can I still want to play?
Yes. Can I still want to stop?
How does Tess finish the conversation?
Tell her both answers are yes
You play. I stop. We both get to want what we want, and nobody has to earn it.
Yes. To all of it. I’m keeping the fern flyer.
The hatchback finally closes. They both cheer like it was a jam.
Tess and Camille agreed both choices are valid—Camille keeps playing, Tess stops.
Offer the market—as friends, for now
Come to the market. As friends. No pressure, just a very long line for succulents.
Friends who get up at eight on a Sunday. That’s a big ask.
I’ll set an alarm.
Tess invited Camille to the plant market as friends; Camille said she’d set an alarm.
Take the flyer back—bad timing
I take the flyer back and fold it into my pocket. ‘Forget it. Bad timing.’
Okay. If you ever want to un-forget it, I like ferns more than I let on.
Tess took the market flyer back; Camille said she likes ferns more than she lets on.
What Tonight Is
Tess decides: skate, or watch
Millbrook Rink, bout night
Saturday, 6:30 PM
Last home bout of the season. Tess’s last one, either way. The bleachers are full. Her gear is in her bag. Her knee has its own opinion.
I sit in the locker room with one skate laced and one not. The knee’s a three out of ten tonight. Yesterday it was a six.
I crouch in front of her. I’m not the coach. I don’t get a vote. I say so out loud.
Tell me what tonight is.
An ending. Not all of them.
Whatever you pick, I’ll find you after the last jam. Track or bench.
She isn’t asking me to play. She isn’t asking me not to. For once, my body gets to answer first.
What does Tess choose tonight?
Skate one last jam—then sit
One jam, if the medic clears me. Then I’m done, and I mean it.
The coach and the medic both say yes. Tess blocks one jam—one—and Camille scores through the gap she opens. Then Tess sits, and the rink loses its mind.
I skate my lap past the bench, slow, so she can high-five me.
Cleared by coach and medic, Tess skated one last jam and then sat; Camille scored through her block.
Watch from the bench in your jersey
I’m watching. From the bench. Jersey on, skates off.
Good. Then I know exactly where to look.
Tess cheers so loud the ref glances over. It’s the best game she’s ever not played.
Tess watched her last bout from the bench in her jersey.
Skip the bout and go home
I can’t watch it. Not tonight. I’ll be at the party.
That’s allowed. I’ll tell you the score if you want it. I won’t if you don’t.
Tess repots a snake plant at eleven p.m. Camille texts one word: ‘Won.’ Then: ‘Missed you. Not a guilt trip.’
Tess skipped the bout; Camille texted the result without guilt.
How to Fall
Hear a speech that doesn’t decide her life for her
Back room, the Duckpin bar and lanes
Saturday the 23rd, 9:15 PM
The retirement party, in the back room of the team’s bowling-alley bar. Streamers, a sheet cake shaped like a knee pad, and Camille at the mic with no notes.
I’m not going to tell you what Tess does next. That’s her business. I’m going to tell you what she did.
She taught me how to fall. Then how to get up without pretending it didn’t hurt.
The room goes quiet the way a rink goes quiet before a whistle. Then everybody’s yelling, which is correct.
I find her by the pinball machine afterward. My face is doing something I can’t manage.
The Riverside market. Tomorrow at eight. It has absolutely no competitive value.
I’ve never asked her anywhere that didn’t have a scoreboard. My hands are worse than before any bout.
What does Tess do after the speech?
Tell her what the speech meant
You didn’t tell them who I am now. You let me decide that. It’s the nicest thing anyone’s ever said about me into a microphone.
Eight o’clock. I’ll be the one yawning.
Tess told Camille the speech meant everything because it left her future to her; Camille said yes to the market.
Make the market a group outing
Actually—bring whoever. Dee, too. Big team plant trip.
Sure. But I’m riding with you.
It’s a softer invitation. Camille hears the door left in it and doesn’t push on it.
Tess widened the market trip to the team; Camille said she’d ride with her.
Thank her, then leave the party
Thank you. Really. I need some air—and probably a night alone.
Go. You earned the exit.
The market invitation hangs in the air—not accepted, not taken back.
Tess thanked Camille and left early; the market invitation was left open.
No Score at the Market
Find a date that doesn’t need a scoreboard
Riverside Plant Market
Sunday, 8:20 AM
Sunday morning. Folding tables, grow lights, a man who sells only cacti and has named every one. Camille carries three pots. Tess walks slower than her, on purpose now.
Do we keep score here?
Only how many pots you carry.
I carry four. I’m not proud of it. I’m a little proud of it.
I want another morning.
Before or after practice?
A day we both choose.
Then that can be a date.
What does Tess say to another morning?
Call it a date—and pick the day
It’s a date. Monday—your rest day, my every day. The botanical garden. I drive, you carry.
Deal. Can I hold your hand here, or is that a penalty?
I hold out my hand. It’s not a penalty. It’s a decision.
Tess and Camille set a date—Monday, the botanical garden—and held hands at the market.
Say friends for now—more mornings, slowly
More mornings. As friends, for now. I’m new at not being a derby player. I want to learn one new thing at a time.
Then I’ll be the slowest friend you’ve ever had.
Tess asked to keep it to friendly mornings for now; Camille agreed to go slow.
Say this is the goodbye—kindly
I think this was the goodbye I needed. Not to you—to us as teammates. I don’t think there’s a next thing.
I hand her the fourth pot. It was hers anyway. I bought it for her.
Okay. I’m glad it was a plant and not a scoreboard.
Tess told Camille there’s no next step; Camille accepted it and gave her the plant.
Two Pots
Choose what life off the track looks like
Tess’s apartment, the windowsill
Three weeks later, Sunday, 5:00 PM
Three weeks later. Tess’s windowsill holds seven plants and one retired knee pad working as a saucer. Camille comes by after an away bout, still smelling like the rink.
I set down a new pot: the fern from the flyer. Found it at a hardware store in a town we lost in.
We lost by forty. I didn’t care as much as I used to. That scared me a little.
That’s allowed. So is caring. You don’t have to quit because I did.
I’m not quitting. I’ve got two more seasons in me, maybe three. I’d like you in the stands for some of them. Not all.
Some. Not all. It’s the most honest schedule anyone has ever offered me.
What does Tess choose?
Say yes—different schedules, one calendar
Yes. Some bouts, most Mondays, all the markets.
And the rest of the time we’re just two women with too many plants.
I kiss her by the windowsill, next to the fern. Nobody is keeping score.
Tess and Camille became a couple on different schedules: some bouts, most Mondays, all the markets.
Stay friends—keep the door open
I need a season of just me. Friends. Real ones. Ask me again in spring?
Spring. I’ll bring a plant as a reminder. Passive-aggressive gardening.
The fern stays on the sill. So does the question.
Tess chose friendship for now and asked Camille to ask again in spring.
Pause it—and stay teammates at heart
You’re all the way in. I’m all the way out. I don’t think we fit right now, and I won’t make you smaller to try.
I’d have tried.
I know. That’s why I’m saying it.
At the team’s farewell banquet a month later, they sit at the same table and toast each other, and mean it.
Tess paused the private relationship; they stayed gracious teammates at the farewell banquet.
